title: Short-Channel Effects and Device Models
intro: The square law of the early chapters is accurate only for long channels. This chapter covers what changes as devices shrink and how simulators model it (Razavi, Chapter 17).

blocks.text: Why it matters to an analog designer

items: Scaling made digital logic faster, cheaper and lower in power, but it lowered supply voltages and squeezed the swing and dynamic range of analog circuits.
Short channels bend the I/V curves: threshold depends on L and $V_{DS}$, mobility falls with gate field, carriers saturate in velocity, and $r_O$ varies with $V_{DS}$.
Circuits are designed in SPICE, so the device model (and its corners) decides how well simulation predicts silicon. Knowing the effects helps explain odd simulation results.
Scaling Theory: constant-field and constant-voltage scaling, and what they do to digital and analog circuits.
Threshold Voltage Effects: subthreshold slope, threshold roll-off, DIBL and the reverse short-channel effect.
Mobility, Velocity Saturation and Output Resistance: vertical and lateral field effects, hot carriers, and how $r_O$ really behaves.
Device Models and Process Corners: Level 1 to 3, BSIM, EKV, charge modelling, temperature and corners.

blocks.title: Which effect?
blocks.text: A designer doubles L of a current-source transistor to raise $r_O$ and finds its $V_{GS}$ for the same current rose by 120 mV. Which short-channel effect explains the surprise?
solution: Threshold roll-off: at minimum length the source and drain depletion regions do part of the gate's job, lowering $V_{TH}$. A longer device loses this help, so $V_{TH}$ (and $V_{GS}$) rises, by 100 to 200 mV in some processes.
